From 1933 to 1935 Telefunken brought out 200 of them. Sala and Paul Hindemith performed in public in 1930, and in 1931 Sala played the solo in Hindemith's concerto for trautonium and string quartet and also premiered Harald Genzmer's concerto for trautonium and orchestra. Sala later added a tuning switch, noise and envelope generators, formant filters and a subharmonic oscillator, forming the mixed trautonium, and it was used in film, on tour and in New York ballet.

The Trautonium is an electrophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 531.1. It does not sound by keyboard: the player presses a finger on a resistance wire above a metal plate, and the position of the contact sets the pitch, while sliding, the pressure of the finger and a pedal control volume, vibrato, portamento and the proportion of filtering. It was invented in Berlin in 1930 by Friedrich Trautwein and developed further by Oskar Sala; it can be used in new-music performances, concertos, film and performances at Bayreuth.
特勞托尼琴的音色具有獨特的電子質感，介於溫潤與詭異之間。其音色明亮而富有穿透力，: The trautonium has a distinctive electronic timbre, somewhere between warm and uncanny. It is bright and penetrating, with a faint metallic sheen and the character of electronic noise. The instrument's range is wide, covering everything from bass to treble. Its resonance comes entirely from electronic circuits and has none of the harmonic resonance of a traditional wooden instrument. Compared with the warm sweetness of a violin, the trautonium is colder and more avant-garde; compared with an organ its tone is finer and more experimental. Its unusual portamento control gives the instrument smooth pitch transitions, so it can produce a continuous, voice-like sound that a traditional keyboard instrument struggles to achieve.

特勞託尼琴屬電鳴樂器，發聲原理為電阻線與金屬板觸控、振盪器與濾波器；地區見於歐洲: The trautonium is an electrophone; it sounds through the touch of a resistance wire on a metal plate, through oscillators and filters, and it belongs to Europe, the USA and the modern recording studio worldwide. The source mentions its use in public concerts, concertos and trio line-ups, such as Hindemith's Concerto for Trautonium and String Quartet and Genzmer's Concerto for Trautonium and Orchestra; it also appears in industrial film, the bird calls of Hitchcock's The Birds, the gong and cymbal bells of Strauss's Japanese Festival Music, the bells of Wagner's Parsifal, Balanchine's ballet Electron, music theatre, film scores and albums.
特勞託尼琴的來源資料未載明琴身或外殼材質，僅能確認其手操部件為金屬板上的電阻線，: The sources on the trautonium do not state the material of the body or casing; all that can be confirmed is that the part the hand works is a resistance wire over a metal plate, the player pressing the wire into contact with the plate. The sound-generating circuit used neon-tube relaxation oscillators at first and later thyratrons and transistors; the output passes through two parallel resonant filter circuits, and a pedal controls the volume before it reaches the amplifier. The materials of the other parts are not stated.
